# Safe Margins

Guided areas ensuring important visuals aren't cut off.

## What are the safe margins in Adobe Premiere Pro?

Safe margins in Adobe Premiere Pro refer to the "safe areas" on the screen where you can place text or graphics to ensure they are fully visible on all types of screens. These margins are especially important when creating content for television, as some TVs may cut off the edges of the video, causing any text or graphics near the edge to be partially or fully obscured.

There are two types of safe margins: Action Safe and Title Safe.
The Action Safe margin is typically set at 5% from each edge of the screen, while the Title Safe margin is set at 10%. Anything within the Title Safe area is guaranteed to be visible on all screens. Anything between the Title Safe area and the Action Safe area is usually visible, but could potentially be cut off on some screens. Anything outside the Action Safe area is likely to be cut off. These margins can be adjusted in the program monitor settings in Adobe Premiere Pro.

## How to set safe margins in Adobe Premiere Pro?

Setting safe margins in Adobe Premiere Pro is a straightforward process. First, open your project in Adobe Premiere Pro. Then, go to the "Program Monitor" and click on the "Wrench" icon, which is also known as the "Settings" button. In the drop-down menu, select "Safe Margins". This will display the safe margins on your video.

The safe margins consist of two rectangles.
The outer rectangle is the "Action Safe" area where you should keep all your important action within. The inner rectangle is the "Title Safe" area where you should keep all your text and graphics within. This ensures that your content will not be cut off when displayed on different screens. You can adjust these margins as needed, but a common practice is to set the action safe area at 90% and the title safe area at 80% of the screen size.

## Why are safe margins important in Adobe Premiere Pro?

Safe margins in Adobe Premiere Pro are important for ensuring that all important content is visible when the video is displayed on different screens. Not all screens display video content in the same way, and some may [crop](../features/video-cropping) or cut off the edges of the video. By keeping all essential content within the safe margins, you can ensure that it will be visible regardless of the display.
Additionally, safe margins also help in maintaining a professional and clean look in your videos. They provide a guideline for aligning text and graphics, ensuring that they are not too close to the edge of the screen where they could be cut off or look cramped. This is particularly important for content that will be broadcasted on television, as different TV models have varying display settings.

## How to adjust safe margins in Adobe Premiere Pro?

To adjust safe margins in Adobe Premiere Pro, first, open the program and select the sequence you want to adjust. Then, go to the "Program Monitor" and click on the "Wrench" icon located at the bottom right of the panel. From the drop-down menu, select "Safe Margins". This will display the safe margins on your sequence.

The safe margins consist of two rectangles. The outer rectangle represents the "Action Safe" area, which is 90% of the total frame. The inner rectangle represents the "Title Safe" area, which is 80% of the total frame.
These areas are guidelines to ensure that important content is not cut off when displayed on different screens. To adjust these margins, you will need to adjust your content to fit within these areas. Unfortunately, Adobe Premiere Pro does not allow you to customize the size of the safe margins.

### Basic Scene and Layout Planning

Before adding chat, decide where it should appear on screen. Chat placement affects readability and overall stream balance. Poor placement can block gameplay or important visual elements.

Think about:

* Whether chat will be visible all the time or only in certain scenes
* If it should sit beside gameplay, under a camera, or in a sidebar

### Appropriate Stream Resolution and Canvas Size

### Adjusting Colors for Readability and Brand Consistency

Chat text color should contrast strongly with your background. This is especially important if your gameplay or camera feed has frequent color changes.

Many overlay tools allow separate color controls for:

* Username text
* Message text
* Moderator, subscriber, or VIP roles

If your stream has a defined color palette, use it sparingly. Overusing brand colors can reduce readability and make chat visually noisy.

### Setting Backgrounds and Transparency Levels

A transparent or semi-transparent chat background keeps the overlay from blocking important content. Full transparency works well only when the underlying video is visually simple.

For most streams, a slightly darkened background improves readability without drawing attention.

Best practices for transparency:

* Use 60–85% transparency for dark chat backgrounds
* Avoid pure black or pure white backgrounds
* Test visibility during bright and dark gameplay moments

## Testing Your Twitch Chat Overlay Before Going Live

Testing your chat overlay ensures it behaves exactly as expected under real streaming conditions. Skipping this step can lead to invisible messages, broken animations, or chat covering important on-screen elements.

A proper test checks both visual appearance and live behavior. Treat this like a rehearsal, not a quick preview.

### Step 1: Use OBS Studio Mode for Safe Testing

Enable Studio Mode in OBS to preview your chat overlay without pushing changes live. This allows you to adjust placement, size, and cropping while keeping your live output unchanged.

### Chat Overlay Covers Important Gameplay Elements

Poor placement can block HUD elements, subtitles, or critical UI. This is especially noticeable in competitive or text-heavy games.

Reposition the overlay:

* Move chat to unused screen edges or corners
* Use opacity or background transparency
* Create a separate scene layout for different games

Testing placement per game prevents readability issues during live streams.

Regular maintenance reduces the chance of mid-stream chat failures.

### Chat Looks Fine in OBS but Not on Stream

This typically means the chat is visible in preview but not included in the active scene being streamed. Scene selection mistakes are common during transitions.

Double-check:

* The correct scene is live in OBS
* The chat overlay source exists in that scene
* Studio Mode transitions are applied properly

Always verify the live output rather than relying only on the preview window.

## Best Practices for a Clean and Streamer-Friendly Chat Overlay

A well-designed chat overlay improves viewer interaction without distracting from gameplay or your on-camera presence. Clean overlays are easier to read, easier to moderate, and more professional-looking over long streams. These best practices help you balance visibility, performance, and aesthetics.
### Prioritize Readability Over Style

Fancy animations and custom fonts can look impressive, but they often reduce readability during fast-moving chats. Viewers should be able to read messages instantly, even on mobile screens.

Stick to:

* Sans-serif fonts like Inter, Roboto, or Arial
* Font sizes large enough to read at 720p
* High contrast between text and background

If viewers need to squint or pause the stream, the overlay is too complex.

### Limit the Number of Visible Messages

Displaying too many messages at once creates visual clutter and pulls attention away from the content. A smaller message stack keeps the overlay tidy and focused.

A good rule of thumb is:

* 4 to 8 visible messages for fast chats
* 6 to 10 messages for slower, community streams

Older messages should fade out smoothly rather than disappearing abruptly.

### Use Subtle Backgrounds or Transparency

Chat text floating directly over gameplay can become unreadable during bright or fast scenes.
A subtle background improves contrast without blocking important visuals.

Effective options include:

* Semi-transparent dark boxes
* Blurred background panels
* Gradient fades behind text only

Avoid solid blocks that cover HUD elements or critical gameplay areas.

### Place Chat Where It Does Not Compete With Content

Chat placement should feel intentional, not squeezed into leftover space. Poor positioning is one of the most common mistakes new streamers make.

Best placement guidelines:

* Avoid minimaps, health bars, and scoreboards
* Keep chat away from facecam framing
* Test placement across different game genres

What works for a shooter may not work for a strategy or horror game.

### Design With Moderation in Mind

A clean overlay is also a moderated one. Spam, long messages, and excessive emotes can quickly overwhelm the screen.

Most overlay tools allow you to:

* Limit emote-only messages
* Restrict message length
* Hide first-time chatter or links
